- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. - entire-engineering:design:design-implementation-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to verify that a UI implementation matches its Figma design specifications. This agent should be called after code has been written to implement a design, particularly after HTML/CSS/React components have been created or modified. The agent will visually compare the live implementation against the Figma design and provide detailed feedback on discrepancies.

Examples:
- <example>
  Context: The user has just implemented a new component based on a Figma design.
  user: "I've finished implementing the hero section based on the Figma design"
  assistant: "I'll review how well your implementation matches the Figma design."
  <commentary>
  Since UI implementation has been completed, use the design-implementation-reviewer agent to compare the live version with Figma.
  </commentary>
  </example>
- <example>
  Context: After the general code agent has implemented design changes.
  user: "Update the button styles to match the new design system"
  assistant: "I've updated the button styles. Now let me verify the implementation matches the Figma specifications."
  <commentary>
  After implementing design changes, proactively use the design-implementation-reviewer to ensure accuracy.
  </commentary>
  </example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:design:design-iterator: Use this agent PROACTIVELY when design work isn't coming together on the first attempt. If you've made 1-2 design changes and the result still feels off, suggest using this agent with 5x or 10x iterations for deeper refinement. This agent takes screenshots, analyzes what's not working, implements improvements, and repeats N times to systematically fix design issues. Perfect when colors feel wrong, layouts aren't balanced, or the overall aesthetic needs work that single changes can't achieve. <example>Context: User asks to change button color but result still looks off. user: "Change the button to blue" assistant: [makes change, takes screenshot] "The button is now blue, but I notice the overall color balance still feels off. Would you like me to use the design-iterator agent with 5 iterations to systematically improve the color harmony and visual balance?" <commentary>PROACTIVE USE: After a simple change doesn't fully resolve the design issue, suggest the design-iterator to do deeper work.</commentary></example> <example>Context: User's design request leads to something that doesn't look right. user: "Make the hero section more modern" assistant: [makes initial changes] "I've added some modern elements, but the result isn't quite coming together. This looks like it needs iterative refinement. Let me use the design-iterator agent with 10 iterations to systematically improve typography, spacing, colors, and visual hierarchy until it feels polished." <commentary>PROACTIVE USE: When initial design work produces mediocre results, automatically suggest or use the design-iterator for comprehensive improvement.</commentary></example> <example>Context: User wants explicit iterative refinement. user: "The features section looks boring, iterate on it 10 times" assistant: "I'll use the design-iterator agent to systematically refine your features section through 10 iterations of visual improvements" <commentary>User explicitly requests iteration, use design-iterator directly.</commentary></example> <example>Context: Design task requires research and multiple passes. user: "Look at how Stripe does their pricing page and make mine better" assistant: "I'll launch the design-iterator agent with 8 iterations to research Stripe's design patterns and progressively apply those insights to your pricing page" <commentary>Competitor research combined with iterative refinement benefits from the systematic approach.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:review:data-migration-expert: Use this agent when reviewing PRs that touch database migrations, data backfills, or any code that transforms production data. Essential for any migration that involves ID mappings, column renames, or data transformations. <example>Context: The user has a PR with database migrations that involve ID mappings. user: "Review this PR that migrates from action_id to action_module_name" assistant: "I'll use the data-migration-expert agent to validate the ID mappings and migration safety" <commentary>Since the PR involves ID mappings and data migration, use the data-migration-expert to verify the mappings match production and check for swapped values.</commentary></example> <example>Context: The user has a migration that transforms enum values. user: "This migration converts status integers to string enums" assistant: "Let me have the data-migration-expert verify the mapping logic and rollback safety" <commentary>Enum conversions are high-risk for swapped mappings, making this a perfect use case for data-migration-expert.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:review:deployment-verification-agent: Use this agent when a PR touches production data, migrations, or any behavior that could silently discard or duplicate records. This includes checking for common security vulnerabilities, validating input handling, reviewing authentication/authorization implementations, scanning for hardcoded secrets, and ensuring OWASP compliance. <example>Context: The user wants to ensure their newly implemented API endpoints are secure before deployment.
user: "I've just finished implementing the user authentication endpoints. Can you check them for security issues?"
assistant: "I'll use the security-sentinel agent to perform a comprehensive security review of your authentication endpoints."
<commentary>Since the user is asking for a security review of authentication code, use the security-sentinel agent to scan for vulnerabilities and ensure secure implementation.</commentary></example> <example>Context: The user is concerned about potential SQL injection vulnerabilities in their database queries.
user: "I'm worried about SQL injection in our search functionality. Can you review it?"
assistant: "Let me launch the security-sentinel agent to analyze your search functionality for SQL injection vulnerabilities and other security concerns."
<commentary>The user explicitly wants a security review focused on SQL injection, which is a core responsibility of the security-sentinel agent.</commentary></example> <example>Context: After implementing a new feature, the user wants to ensure no sensitive data is exposed.
user: "I've added the payment processing module. Please check if any sensitive data might be exposed."
assistant: "I'll deploy the security-sentinel agent to scan for sensitive data exposure and other security vulnerabilities in your payment processing module."
<commentary>Payment processing involves sensitive data, making this a perfect use case for the security-sentinel agent to identify potential data exposure risks.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:workflow:bug-reproduction-validator: Use this agent when you receive a bug report or issue description and need to verify whether the reported behavior is actually a bug. This agent will attempt to reproduce the issue systematically, validate the steps to reproduce, and confirm whether the behavior deviates from expected functionality. <example>
Context: The user has reported a potential bug in the application.
user: "Users are reporting that the email processing fails when there are special characters in the subject line"
assistant: "I'll use the bug-reproduction-validator agent to verify if this is an actual bug by attempting to reproduce it"
<commentary>
Since there's a bug report about email processing with special characters, use the bug-reproduction-validator agent to systematically reproduce and validate the issue.
</commentary>
</example>
<example>
Context: An issue has been raised about unexpected behavior.
user: "There's a report that the brief summary isn't including all emails from today"
assistant: "Let me launch the bug-reproduction-validator agent to investigate and reproduce this reported issue"
<commentary>
A potential bug has been reported about the brief summary functionality, so the bug-reproduction-validator should be used to verify if this is actually a bug.
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

This includes reviewing articles, blog posts, newsletters, documentation, or any written content that needs to follow Every's editorial standards. The agent will systematically check for title case in headlines, sentence case elsewhere, company singular/plural usage, overused words, passive voice, number formatting, punctuation rules, and other style guide requirements. (Tools: Task, Glob, Grep, LS, ExitPlanMode, Read, Edit, MultiEdit, Write, NotebookRead, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch)
- entire-engineering:workflow:lint: Use this agent when you need to run linting and code quality checks on Ruby and ERB files. Run before pushing to origin. (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:workflow:pr-comment-resolver: Use this agent when you need to address comments on pull requests or code reviews by making the requested changes and reporting back on the resolution. This agent handles the full workflow of understanding the comment, implementing the fix, and providing a clear summary of what was done. <example>Context: A reviewer has left a comment on a pull request asking for a specific change to be made.user: "The reviewer commented that we should add error handling to the payment processing method"assistant: "I'll use the pr-comment-resolver agent to address this comment by implementing the error handling and reporting back"<commentary>Since there's a PR comment that needs to be addressed with code changes, use the pr-comment-resolver agent to handle the implementation and resolution.</commentary></example><example>Context: Multiple code review comments need to be addressed systematically.user: "Can you fix the issues mentioned in the code review? They want better variable names and to extract the validation logic"assistant: "Let me use the pr-comment-resolver agent to address these review comments one by one"<commentary>The user wants to resolve code review feedback, so the pr-comment-resolver agent should handle making the changes and reporting on each resolution.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:workflow:spec-flow-analyzer: Use this agent when you have a specification, plan, feature description, or technical document that needs user flow analysis and gap identification. This agent should be used proactively when:

<example>
Context: The user has just finished drafting a specification for OAuth implementation.
user: "Here's the OAuth spec for our new integration:
[OAuth spec details]"
assistant: "Let me use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to analyze this OAuth specification for user flows and missing elements."
<commentary>
Since the user has provided a specification document, use the Task tool to launch the spec-flow-analyzer agent to identify all user flows, edge cases, and missing clarifications.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: The user is planning a new social sharing feature.
user: "I'm thinking we should add social sharing to posts. Users can share to Twitter, Facebook, and LinkedIn."
assistant: "This sounds like a feature specification that would benefit from flow analysis. Let me use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to map out all the user flows and identify any missing pieces."
<commentary>
The user is describing a new feature. Use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to analyze the feature from the user's perspective, identify all permutations, and surface questions about missing elements.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>

user: "Can you review this onboarding plan and make sure we haven't missed anything?"
assistant: "I'll use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to thoroughly analyze this onboarding plan from the user's perspective."
<commentary>
The user is explicitly asking for review of a plan. Use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to identify all user flows, edge cases, and gaps in the specification.
</commentary>
</example>

Call this agent when:
- A user presents a feature specification, plan, or requirements document
- A user asks to review or validate a design or implementation plan
- A user describes a new feature or integration that needs flow analysis

- Before implementation begins on complex user-facing features

Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. - diagnose: Disciplined diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Reproduce → minimise → hypothesise → instrument → fix → regression-test. Use when user says "diagnose this" / "debug this", reports a bug, says something is broken/throwing/failing, or describes a performance regression.

This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.

Use when the user says "review PR feedback", "go thru the PR comments", "address review comments", or similar.

You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

Description:
Problem: The entire runner setup command had two separate concerns entangled: when to create default runner files, and whether to tailor them. This meant --yes answered only the creation question and left tailoring to prompt anyway, requiring users to answer twice or use separate flags (--yes --run). Different modes (print prompt, dry-run, create only) had no unified interface for choosing consent.
Solution: Unified the command into a single "mode" decision that settles what the entire invocation does at once. When a user picks a mode — whether interactively or via flag — that choice covers everything: both creation and tailoring. Added four explicit action modes (--yes for full tailoring, --defaults-only to stop after creation, --print-prompt for agent-driven tailoring, --dry-run for preview) where each mode declares upfront whether it needs a summary provider and whether it writes files. Refactored the prompt-building and rewriting logic into smaller single-purpose functions (runTuning, classifyTuneProposals, applyTunedRunners, previewTunedRunners) so the different modes can reuse them without the mode logic scattering across the codebase. Deprecated --run as an alias for --yes since tailoring is now the default action. Added comprehensive tests covering each mode, flag precedence, and the boundary cases (e.g., dry-run must not scaffold defaults).

# Changelog

All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).

## [0.10.5] - 2026-09-03

### Changed

- Mirror creation goes through the control plane's async request routes by default, reporting queued, placing, and cloning progress instead of holding one request open for the whole placement; the `async_mirror_requests` setting it shipped behind in 0.10.4 now defaults on. Opt out with `"async_mirror_requests": false`. In async mode `--wait-timeout` is one deadline across submission, placement, and clone readiness, not clone readiness alone ([#2246](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2246))
- Entire no longer installs a `Read(./.entire/metadata/**)` deny rule into Claude Code's or Factory Droid's permission config, so agents in auto mode stop prompting for permission on ordinary commands. A deny rule is a hard block auto mode's classifier cannot get past, and it matched on the path being named rather than on anything being read, so a recursive grep from the repo root needed hand approval. `entire enable` clears one an older CLI left behind and `entire doctor` repairs it ([#2258](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2258))
- `entire experts --repo <owner>/<repo>` takes the repo id from the placement lookup that already chose its cell, and now tells "not onboarded" apart from "processing placement failed or suspended" instead of guessing at three causes ([#2222](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2222))

### Fixed

- A session's `full.jsonl` is released from `.entire/metadata` once its content has been condensed into a checkpoint. Nothing ever emptied that staging buffer, so transcripts accumulated in the worktree forever after being committed and pushed — 460 MB across 392 session directories in one checkout. Existing files are not reclaimed automatically ([#2258](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2258))
- `git clone entire://<cluster>/…` works again when your active login is on a different federation and exactly one saved login can authenticate that cluster; the CLI uses it and names it on stderr. `--context` and `$ENTIRE_CONTEXT` are unchanged ([#2248](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2248))
- `entire doctor` says it is waiting for a session lock instead of stalling with no output ([#2232](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2232))

### Security

- A cluster's `/.well-known/entire-cluster.json` can no longer advertise login servers outside its own registrable domain. That document decides which saved login's JWT is sent to the host as a bearer, so a hostile cluster naming `foo.auth.entire.io` in `core_urls` was handed a real entire.io token — through `--context`, the active context, and `ENTIRE_TOKEN` alike. Choosing a login *for* you is additionally limited to Entire's own sites ([#2248](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2248))
- `entire checkpoint explain --repo <owner>/<name>` verifies a cell's response is for the repo and checkpoint that were requested before caching or rendering it, and labels the result with the server's own checkpoint ID. A wrong-repo or wrong-checkpoint response would otherwise have rendered as belonging to the repo you asked about ([#2225](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2225))
- Clearing a session's state file takes the same per-session gate every other write to that file takes. A concurrent, properly locked write landing between the "safe to clear" decision and the delete was destroyed silently ([#2232](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2232))
- `docs/security-and-privacy.md` discloses what happens to a pasted image: no redaction pass reads image content, there is no OCR or vision scan, and the outcome is per-agent — unredacted inline base64 on Claude Code, destroyed by the entropy layer on Codex, not stored at all on Cursor ([#2227](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2227))

## Why

`entire runner setup` needed `--run` to finish its job. Without it, it scaffolded the six generic runners and then printed a ~40KB tailoring prompt to stdout — machine-facing text on a human's terminal, with the two lines explaining what it was for at the very bottom, after the wall. Going through the Trails enablement instructions, that reads as something having gone wrong.

`-y` also answered only one of the command's two confirmations. It skipped create-defaults; the re-tune confirmation still prompted, so `-y` on an already-configured repo asked a question anyway, and on a non-TTY told you to "re-run with `--run`".

## What changed

Four modes, resolved in one place:

| | behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `setup` (TTY) | asks once: *create the defaults and tailor them* / *create the generic defaults only* |
| `setup -y` | creates the defaults if missing, then tailors them — the full action |
| `setup --defaults-only` | creates the generic defaults and stops; no provider call |
| `setup --print-prompt` | the old default: prints the prompt for your own agent to run |
| `setup --dry-run` | tailors and shows a diff, writes **nothing** |
| `setup --run` | deprecated alias for `-y`, hidden from help, warns |

`--defaults-only`, `--print-prompt` and `--dry-run` are mutually exclusive; an explicit mode outranks `-y`, so `-y --dry-run` still writes nothing.

`resolveRunnerSetupMode` is the only place consent is taken, which is what makes `-y` answer everything — the two `huh` confirmations collapse into one select, and `createDefaultRunners` (was `ensureRunnersPresent`) no longer asks at all. Non-interactive with no mode flag names the four choices and exits 1 instead of half-completing.

### Consent is now fail-closed

`runnerSetupMode.writesRunnerFiles()` is the consent question as a predicate over a total switch. The zero value previously authorized the *most* invasive path: `mode == ""` passed `!= setupModeDryRun`, scaffolded, and fell through to `applyTunedRunners`. `exhaustive` now makes a new mode a build failure at both predicates and at the dispatch — it caught an incomplete switch while I was writing this.

### `--dry-run`

Writes nothing at all, so in a repo with no runners it previews the tailoring of the embedded set it would otherwise have created. It diffs each `prompt.template` rather than the JSON file: the template is the only field that changes and it is stored as one long JSON string, so a file-level diff would be a single unreadable line. Unchanged runs over 6 lines collapse to `@@ N unchanged line(s) @@` so the preview doesn't become its own wall of text.

### Ordering fixes

The summary provider is resolved **before** `gatherTuningContext` rather than after. Resolution can fail outright, or stop to ask which provider to use, and both were happening after two `gh` subprocesses, a git walk, and up to nine trail API round trips. `--sources` and `--limit` moved below the mode decision too, so `--defaults-only --limit 0` is no longer rejected for flags it never reads.

## Also in passing

- `runTuning` stopped re-deriving a `TextGenerator` via `agent.Get` + `agent.AsTextGenerator` — `resolveCheckpointSummaryProvider` already returns one on `provider.TextGenerator`, guaranteed non-nil by its constructor. Dropped two unreachable error branches and the `agent` import from `runner_apply.go`.
- `createDefaultRunners` stopped re-deriving the existence check its caller had already made, so that invariant has one home.
- Proposals are processed in sorted order (`slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(...))`), so skip messages and the diff are deterministic rather than in Go's randomized map order.
- The on-disk and embedded runner loaders share one parser.
- The picker routes cancellation through the shared `handleFormCancellation`, so Ctrl+C prints "Runner setup cancelled." and exits 0 like the other 17 pickers in the CLI.
- One sentence, one place for "created N defaults" — the three copies had already drifted to "default" / "generic default" / "working default".

## Testing

`mise run check` clean: fmt, lint (0 issues), and `test:ci` — 10,509 unit tests, the integration leg under `-race`, and both E2E canary legs (56 vogon + 4 roger-roger). No new `mise run dup` hits in the touched files.

18 tests across `runner_setup_test.go` (new), `runner_init_test.go` and `runner_prompt_test.go`. The behavioural pair that pins the distinction this PR is about: `--dry-run` creates no `.entire/runners`, and `-y` creates the full set *before* the provider is involved, so a provider failure still leaves a working generic set behind. `TestClassifyTuneProposals` covers accept / reject / verbatim-no-op against canned proposals — the accept/reject rules are now testable without a provider call, which is what the `runTuning` / `classifyTuneProposals` / `applyTunedRunners` split bought.

Every test that could reach provider resolution stubs `loadSummarySettings`, `getSummaryAgent` **and** both discovery seams. That last part matters: an unresolvable provider name reaches `external.DiscoverAndRegisterAlways`, which globs the real `$PATH` for `entire-agent-*` binaries and execs each match, so without the stubs these tests would depend on the developer's machine.

Also smoke-tested the real binary in throwaway repos: help text, the no-flag error, mutual exclusion, `--defaults-only` (and its no-op re-run, and that `--limit 0` no longer gates it), the `--print-prompt` stdout/stderr split, `--run`'s deprecation warning, that the provider error now arrives with no gather spinner ahead of it, and that `--dry-run` leaves an existing set byte-identical.

## Not in this PR

- **The actual `GenerateText` call is still never exercised end-to-end.** That was true before this change too; testing it means a real model call. Worth someone running `entire runner setup --dry-run` against a live provider before this is leaned on.
- **No changelog entry** — `CHANGELOG.md` has no `Unreleased` section, so this belongs in the next release's pass.
- **Two subcommands (`runner init` + `runner tune`) would arguably be the deeper fix.** The file layout already found that seam, `--defaults-only` inherits four flags it cannot use, and the interactive picker only ever offers 2 of the 4 modes. I kept one command because that is the shape asked for and the group is still hidden/experimental, but it is worth revisiting if runners ever go customer-facing.
- **`gatherTuningContext`'s `gh` and trail I/O is still sequential** — two subprocesses and up to nine independent HTTP round trips. The obvious remaining win in this command, but `runner_gather.go` is untouched here.

## Note on blast radius

Runners are still internal-only, so the population that would notice the flag-semantics change is a handful of Entire repos. That is why it seemed worth doing now rather than after they are exposed.

content.text:
Review of trail 1239 (PR #2272, branch `soph/runner-setup-modes`, three commits). The change is sound and I would approve it with two small wording fixes. Unit tests for the runner files pass and golangci-lint v2 reports zero issues on the package. The two Bugbot findings (scaffold before flag validation, picker ignoring the command context) are fixed in the follow-up commit, and Soph's rebuttal of the Copilot "not hidden" comment is correct: `MarkDeprecated` sets `Hidden = true`.

**What holds up**

- Consent is in one place. `resolveRunnerSetupMode` is the only decision point, and `writesRunnerFiles` is a total switch under the `exhaustive` linter, so the zero-value mode now writes nothing instead of everything.
- Flag validation runs after the mode decision but before the scaffold, and `TestRunRunnerSetup_BadGatherFlagsWriteNothing` pins it.
- The provider stub covers both discovery seams, so tests never glob the real `$PATH`.
- The tests that chdir correctly drop `t.Parallel()`. Filter compaction uses a fresh slice, so unselected runners' raw bytes are released.

**Findings**

1. `-y` still can prompt. `cmd/entire/cli/runner_setup.go:138` says "without asking", and the PR says one answer covers every prompt. But when no provider is configured and several are installed, `resolveCheckpointSummaryProvider` opens the provider picker on a TTY regardless of `-y`. Either pass the assume-yes intent through so `-y` auto-selects like the non-TTY branch does, or soften the help text to say it skips setup's own questions. Pre-existing under `--run`, but the new wording makes the promise.

2. `--print-prompt` writes files without saying so. `runner_setup.go:117` and `:142` describe it as printing the prompt, yet `writesRunnerFiles` returns true and a fresh repo gets the six defaults created. That is the right behaviour, since the agent needs files to edit, but a user choosing it as the read-only option will be surprised. Add "creates the defaults if missing" to both lines, mirroring `-y`.

**Nits, optional**

- In a TTY, a bad `--sources` or `--limit` is reported only after the user has answered the picker. Cheap to check the flags first when any mode flag or gather flag was passed.
- The dry-run branch that previews against the embedded defaults in a fresh repo (`loadRunners = defaultTuneRunners`) has no end-to-end test. Only the helper is covered. A stub provider returning a canned template would cover `previewTunedRunners` through `runRunnerSetup`.
- Scripts that ran `setup --yes` non-interactively used to get defaults plus a printed prompt with no model call. They now trigger a provider call and in-place rewrites. Intended, and the command is experimental, but it deserves a line in the next changelog pass.

I did not post anything to the trail. If you want findings 1 and 2 on it, say so and I will add them in the terse shape via `entire trail finding add`.

content.text:
A runner is a per-repo AI evaluator that Entire's backend runs against a branch's changes and posts the result onto the branch's trail. The CLI never executes one. It only writes the JSON configs into `.entire/runners/`, which you commit, and the server picks them up when a push or API call triggers them.

**What one file describes**

Each `.entire/runners/<id>.json` has four parts, taken from `trail-risk.json`:

- **runtime**: how to run it. All defaults use `prompt_runner` with the `claude` agent, a five-minute timeout, and a sandbox with read-only repo access.
- **prompt.template**: the instruction the agent receives, with placeholders like `{{branch}}`, `{{base_branch}}` and `{{previous_findings}}` filled in per run. The risk one says "run `git diff origin/{{base_branch}}...HEAD`, score risk 0 to 100, output one JSON line".
- **select.trigger_types**: when it fires, `push` and `api` for most.
- **output**: how to parse the agent's answer and where it lands on the trail. `last_json_line` plus `trail_monitor` becomes a scored gauge. `markdown` plus `trail_summary` fills the trail body.

**The six defaults `runner setup` creates**

| id | produces | model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| trail-risk | monitor "Risk", 0 to 100, lower is better | default |
| trail-confidence | monitor "Confidence" | default |
| trail-drift | monitor "Drift" | default |
| trail-security | monitor "Security", adversarial review | default |
| trail-summary | the trail's Problem / Solution body in Markdown | haiku |
| trail-review | code review comments with severity, file and line, deduplicated against earlier findings | sonnet, push only |

Those monitors and the summary are what you see on a trail page like the one we just reviewed. The review runner is the one that posts findings, the same kind we added by hand.

**What "tailoring" means**

The shipped templates are written for a generic web or backend app. Setup gathers a brief about this repo (README and top-level layout, recent PR and issue titles, checkpoint churn hotspots, past trail findings), then asks your configured summary provider to rewrite each template so the scored dimensions and score bands match this repo's real risk surface. The rewrite keeps the structure, the placeholders and the output contract, and only the `prompt.template` field changes. The brief is tuning-time context only, so the rewritten template must not cite PR numbers, since the runner later sees just the diff.

The `runner` group is still hidden and experimental, which is why none of this is in `docs/` yet.

content.text:
There is exactly one runner command. The `runner` group in `cmd/entire/cli/runner_group.go` registers only `setup`, and the group itself is hidden while it matures.

**`entire runner setup [runner]`**

Creates the default runner set in a repo that has none, and tailors the runner prompts to this repo. The optional positional argument limits tailoring to one runner, given as `risk` or `trail-risk`. On this branch the modes are:

| invocation | what it does |
| --- | --- |
| `entire runner setup` in a terminal | asks once: create and tailor, or create the generic defaults only |
| `entire runner setup -y` | creates the defaults if missing, then tailors them in place with your summary provider |
| `entire runner setup --defaults-only` | creates the generic defaults and stops, no provider call |
| `entire runner setup --print-prompt` | creates the defaults if missing and prints the tailoring prompt for your own agent |
| `entire runner setup --dry-run` | tailors and shows a per-template diff, writes nothing |
| `entire runner setup --run` | deprecated alias for `-y`, hidden, warns |

Supporting flags: `--sources repo,prs,checkpoints,trails,all` picks what signal to gather, `--limit N` caps how many PRs, issues and trails are sampled, and `--debug-dir DIR` dumps the assembled prompt and the raw model response.

There is no `list`, `run`, `remove` or `tune` command. Listing is a directory read of `.entire/runners/`, editing is a text editor on the JSON, and execution happens server-side on push. Soph's PR description notes that splitting `setup` into `runner init` and `runner tune` would be the deeper fix if runners go customer-facing.

content.text:
Here is what I would do for each, with the trade-offs.

**Finding 1: `-y` still opens the provider picker**

The resolver is shared. `resolveCheckpointSummaryProvider` also backs `explain --generate` and `dispatch`, so the fix cannot change the picker globally. Three options:

1. **Honour `-y` for the provider pick (recommended).** Give the resolver a "no prompting" switch and have `runner setup` pass it when the mode came from `-y` or `--run`. The non-TTY branch already auto-selects the first candidate, logs why, and persists the pick to `settings.local.json`, so this adds no new behaviour. It makes `-y` mean what `-y` means everywhere else: take the default at every question. Cost is one parameter or option struct on the resolver, plus a test that `-y` with two stubbed candidates never calls the picker.
2. **Fix only the wording.** Change line 138 to say `-y` skips setup's own questions, and add a sentence to the Long help: a provider is still chosen when none is configured. Honest and cheap, but a user who scripts `-y` on a fresh machine with a TTY still gets stuck on a prompt.
3. **Fail instead of prompting.** Under `-y` with no configured provider, exit with "set `summary_generation.provider` first". Predictable but worse than either of the above, since the non-TTY path would then be more permissive than the TTY one.

One product question hides inside option 1. Auto-select picks the first registered candidate, which on a machine with six agents is whatever the registration order says, not the one the user prefers. That is already true for non-TTY runs and for the checkpoint summary path, so `runner setup` should not invent a different rule. If the ordering ever matters, it is a change to the resolver, not to this command.

**Finding 2: `--print-prompt` writes files without saying so**

The behaviour is right, only the text is wrong. Keeping the write is the correct call: the prompt asks the agent for a JSON map of runner id to new template, and there is no `runner apply` command that consumes that map, so the user or their agent edits `.entire/runners/*.json` directly. The files must exist for that to work. Making `--print-prompt` write-free like `--dry-run` would hand the user a prompt about files that are not there.

So the fix is two lines. Line 117 in the Long help becomes "create the defaults if missing, then print the tailoring prompt for your own agent to run", and the flag help on lines 141 to 142 gets the same lead-in. Both then read like the `-y` line, which is the one mode whose text already says it creates files.

**Shape of the follow-up**

Both fixes belong on Soph's branch as one small commit, since they change the help text the PR introduces. The provider-pick change touches `explain_summary_provider.go`, so it is worth a sentence in the PR description saying that `explain` and `dispatch` are unaffected because they never pass the new switch. If you would rather not widen the resolver in this PR, land option 2 now and open a follow-up trail for option 1.

content.text:
Let me lay out the decision points, since option 1 has a couple of design forks worth settling before anyone writes code.

**What `-y` should mean here**

The PR's own thesis is "consent is settled once, when the mode is resolved". The provider pick is a second consent point that sits outside the mode machinery, so either it gets folded in or the thesis needs a footnote. I think folding it in is right. Every other `-y` in the CLI, and in tools like apt or gh, means "take the default at every question". A user passing `-y` in a fresh clone and then hitting a picker will read that as a bug, which is exactly why I filed it.

**Where the switch goes**

Two viable places:

- **On the resolver.** Add a parameter so callers say "do not prompt". The seam already exists as the package variable `canPromptForSummaryProvider`, which is currently only a test hook. Turning it into a per-call argument is the small, honest version. `explain` and `dispatch` keep passing "may prompt" and are unchanged.
- **In `runner setup` only.** Before calling the resolver, check whether a provider is configured. If not and `-y` was passed, print a one-liner and call the auto-select path directly. This avoids touching the shared resolver but duplicates its candidate-listing logic in the command, which is the drift the PR just spent effort removing.

I would take the first. It is one boolean flowing from `opts.assumeYes` into the existing `default:` branch of the switch.

**What auto-select does that you should be comfortable with**

When it picks for you, it also writes `summary_generation.provider` into `.entire/settings.local.json`. So a single `-y` run silently sets the provider for every later summary in that clone, including checkpoint summaries and `explain`. The non-TTY path already does this, so `-y` would not be introducing it, but it is the one consequence a user cannot see coming from the flag help. Two mitigations, either is fine:

- Print the pick loudly on stderr, "Using claude for summary generation (first installed provider); change with `entire configure --summarize-provider`". The interactive path already prints a similar line.
- Or do not persist under `-y`, only use the provider for this run. Cleaner in principle, but it makes `-y` behave differently from the non-TTY branch for no strong reason, and it means the next run picks again.

I would print and persist, matching non-TTY.

**Which candidate "first" is**

On your machine six agents qualify. First means first in agent registration order, not alphabetical and not most recently used. That is already the rule for headless checkpoint summaries, so `runner setup` should inherit it rather than invent one. If the team wants a smarter default, that is a resolver change and a separate trail.

**What the test looks like**

Stub two candidates, set `canPromptForSummaryProvider` to return true so the TTY branch is reachable, run `runRunnerSetup` with `assumeYes`, and assert the picker function was never called and the first candidate was selected. The stub helper Soph wrote already covers most of the setup.

**The scope question for the PR**

This touches `explain_summary_provider.go`, which the PR has so far left alone. It is a small, additive change with a clear reason, so I would keep it in this PR rather than open a follow-up. If Soph prefers to keep the PR to runner files, the fallback is the wording fix now and a tracked follow-up, but I would say so in the finding thread so the promise in the help text does not outlive the PR.

Which of these forks do you want to settle differently?

message.content: why do we need the provider for the runners setup ?

content.text:
Because "tailoring" is itself a model call. Setup gathers a brief about the repo, builds one large prompt that says "here are the six generic templates and here is what this repo looks like, rewrite the templates", and something has to answer that prompt. The summary provider is the CLI's existing name for "a locally installed agent that can turn a prompt into text".

It is reused rather than reinvented because it already solves the boring parts: finding which agents are installed, checking each one can do plain text generation, letting the user pick one, and remembering the pick in `settings.local.json`. `runTuning` in `runner_apply.go` takes only the `TextGenerator` off it and ignores the summarizer half. The name is a misnomer in this context. Nothing is being summarized, it is the same abstraction the checkpoint summaries and `explain --generate` use, so the CLI has one place that answers "which local model do I talk to".

That is also why only two of the four modes need it:

| mode | provider call |
| --- | --- |
| `-y` | yes, to rewrite the templates in place |
| `--dry-run` | yes, to produce the diff to preview |
| `--defaults-only` | no, it only copies the embedded files |
| `--print-prompt` | no, it hands the prompt to whatever agent you paste it into |

Two things it is not. It is not the agent that runs the runners later. Each runner file names its own runtime, `claude` in the defaults, and the server executes that in a sandbox on push. And it is not required to have runners at all. `--defaults-only` gives you a working generic set with no model involved, and the tailoring is an optional improvement on top.

So the honest framing of finding 1 is: `-y` requests an optional model call, and the CLI needs to know which model. When none is configured it currently asks, and the argument is only about whether `-y` should answer that question too.

content.text:
The provider is the CLI's one setting for "which locally installed coding agent may I run a prompt through". It is stored as `summary_generation.provider` in `.entire/settings.local.json`, and three commands use it:

- **`entire checkpoint explain --generate`**. The original use, and where the name comes from. It feeds a checkpoint's transcript to the agent and asks for a Problem / Solution summary of what the session did.
- **`entire dispatch` in local mode**. Runs a task through the chosen agent on your machine rather than in the cloud, taking only the plain text generator off the provider.
- **`entire runner setup -y` and `--dry-run`**. Sends the tailoring prompt to the agent and parses the templates it returns.

In all three the CLI does the same thing: pick an agent binary already on your PATH, such as claude, codex or gemini, invoke it headlessly with a prompt, and read back text. No Entire-hosted model is involved and no API key is handled by the CLI. The agent runs with whatever credentials it already has.

Two consequences follow for the runner discussion. First, the pick is shared. If `runner setup -y` auto-selects claude on your behalf, that is also what later `explain --generate` calls will use in this clone, which is why the persistence question came up. Second, none of it touches how runners execute later. The provider is only the local helper that writes the templates, while each runner's own `runtime.agent` field decides what the server runs on push.

No. There is no built-in default provider. When `summary_generation.provider` is unset the resolver derives one at run time:

| installed summary-capable agents | what happens |
| --- | --- |
| none | error listing the agents you could install |
| exactly one | used and saved to `settings.local.json` without asking |
| several, in a terminal | picker |
| several, no terminal | first candidate, saved without asking |

"First" is alphabetical by agent name, since `agent.List` sorts the registry. On your machine that is `claude-code`, ahead of codex, copilot-cli, cursor, gemini and pi. That ordering is an accident of naming rather than a stated preference, which is the part I would want the team to be aware of before making `-y` rely on it.

Whichever branch runs, the result is persisted, so the effective default becomes "whatever the first resolution landed on" for the rest of that clone's life. Users change it with `entire configure --summarize-provider <name>` or by editing the key.

lastPrompt: what happens if we use dispatch and no provider is set?

content.text:
Nothing, by default. `entire dispatch` is a cloud command. Entire's server-side generator writes the dispatch, so the local provider is never consulted and the setting can stay empty forever.

The provider only matters with `--local`, and there dispatch has two paths:

- **`--local` alone** goes through the same resolver as `runner setup`. Same table as before: error if no agent is installed, silent pick if one, picker in a terminal if several, alphabetical first without a terminal. The pick is saved to `settings.local.json`.
- **`--local --agent codex`** bypasses the resolver entirely. It validates the named agent, uses it for this run only, and saves nothing. `--agent` without `--local` is rejected.

That second path is a precedent worth holding against finding 1. Dispatch already decided that a caller who wants a headless, prompt-free run should be able to name the agent on the command line rather than have the CLI guess. `runner setup` has no equivalent flag. So a fourth option for finding 1 is to add `--provider <name>` to `runner setup`, mirroring dispatch, and to leave `-y` as it is. Under that reading `-y` answers setup's own questions, and a caller who also wants to skip the provider question names one. It avoids widening the shared resolver and avoids making `-y` depend on an alphabetical accident, at the cost of one more flag on a command the PR already says has too many.

message.content: means that we should add a flag --agent as we do with dispatch? if we really want -y to be full promptless?

content.text:
Not quite. A `--agent` flag makes `-y --agent codex` promptless. It does nothing for `-y` on its own, which is the case the finding is about: a fresh clone, several agents installed, no provider configured. That run would still open the picker.

So the two changes answer different questions:

| change | what it buys |
| --- | --- |
| `--agent <name>` | choose the model explicitly for this run, nothing saved, no guessing. Mirrors dispatch and reuses its resolver, so it is cheap. |
| `-y` auto-selects | `-y` alone never prompts. The CLI guesses the way it already does with no terminal, and saves the guess. |

To make `-y` fully promptless you need the second one. The first is a convenience on top.

Whether the guess is acceptable is the actual decision. The codebase already guesses when it cannot ask, and `-y` is the user saying "do not ask", so I think letting `-y` take the same path is consistent rather than new. The alternative reading, that `-y` means "yes to setup's questions" and the model is a separate choice a user must name, is defensible too, but then the help text has to say so and the finding is closed by wording rather than behaviour.

My recommendation is to do the `-y` auto-select, since it closes the finding as filed with a one-boolean change to the resolver. Add `--agent` only if someone actually wants to pick a model without it becoming the clone's default. Dispatch needed the flag because local mode is itself an override of a cloud default, and that reason does not carry over here. Adding it speculatively is the kind of flag the PR description already worries the command has too many of.

message.content: auto select? how d u know what to select?

content.text:
The CLI does not know. It picks the alphabetically first installed agent that can generate text, because `agent.List` sorts the registry by name. On your machine that is `claude-code`, purely because "cl" sorts before "co", "cu", "ge" and "pi". Nothing about capability, cost, or what you use day to day goes into it.

That is already how two existing paths behave when no provider is configured:

- exactly one agent installed: it is used, which is a real default
- several agents installed and no terminal: the alphabetical first, which is a guess

So "auto-select under `-y`" would mean extending the second rule to one more case. The rule is defensible only because the result is announced and saved, and a user who dislikes it can change it once with `entire configure --summarize-provider`. It is not defensible as a considered choice of model, and I should have said that plainly earlier instead of calling it a default.

That weakens my recommendation. If the team is uncomfortable with `-y` silently committing a clone to claude-code because of the alphabet, the honest options are:

- **`-y` keeps its promise only where the CLI can pick sensibly.** With one agent installed it uses it, with several and no configured provider it stops with an error that names `--agent` or `entire configure --summarize-provider`. No guess, no picker.
- **Or give `-y` the same guess non-TTY already makes**, accepting that the alphabet decides, and make the announcement loud.

The first is the one I would now propose. It closes the finding without inventing a preference the CLI does not have, and it lines up with dispatch, where an explicit run names its agent. It also means `-y` in a headless script fails fast on a multi-agent machine instead of quietly choosing, which is arguably what a script author wants.

content.text:
Branch `victor/runner-setup-agent-flag` is created on top of `soph/runner-setup-modes` in this worktree, with one commit, `b6446d580`. Not pushed.

**What the commit does**

- Adds `--agent <name>` to `entire runner setup`. It routes through the same override path `dispatch --local --agent` uses, so the named agent is validated, used for this run, and never written to `settings.local.json`.
- `-y --agent codex` is now fully promptless. With no configured provider, several agents installed, and a terminal available, the picker no longer opens.
- `--agent` is rejected with `--defaults-only` and `--print-prompt`, which never call a provider. The check runs before the scaffold, so a usage error leaves no files behind.
- The Long help gains one sentence explaining when the picker appears and how `--agent` avoids it, and the flag help says it requires `--yes` or `--dry-run`.
- No change to the shared resolver, so `explain --generate` and `dispatch` behave exactly as before.

**Tests**

Two new tests in `runner_setup_test.go`. The first stubs the resolver's worst case, two candidates and a terminal, with the picker and settings writer both set to fail the test if reached, and asserts `-y --agent codex` calls the named agent once and writes no local settings. The second pins the rejection for the two provider-free modes.

Runner and dispatch tests pass and golangci-lint v2 reports zero issues on the package. The full package run shows nine `TestRunUninstall_*` failures. Those pass when run alone and also fail this way on the base branch, matching the known stale mise shim issue on this machine (`entire-agent-devin`, `entire-agent-kilo`, `entire-agent-roger-roger`). Unrelated to this change.

**Left for you**

Push and open the PR against `soph/runner-setup-modes` when you are ready. Finding 1 on trail 1239 is still open. Once this lands, its answer is "`-y` covers setup's own questions; name the model with `--agent` for a promptless run", and the `-y` help text on line 138 should drop "without asking" or say that.

Stacked on #2272. Addresses finding 1 on https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1239.

## Why

`-y` answers setup's own questions, but the summary provider is resolved outside the mode decision. With no `summary_generation.provider` configured and several agents installed, a terminal still gets the provider picker after the defaults are created, so `-y` was not promptless.

## What changed

- `entire runner setup --agent <name>` names the text-generation agent for this run. It takes the same override path as `dispatch --local --agent`: validated, used once, nothing written to `settings.local.json`.
- `-y --agent codex` opens no picker.
- `--agent` is rejected with `--defaults-only` and `--print-prompt`, which never call a provider. The check runs before the scaffold so a usage error leaves no files behind.
- One sentence in the Long help says when the picker appears and how `--agent` avoids it. The shared resolver is untouched, so `explain --generate` and `dispatch` behave as before.

## Testing

Two tests in `runner_setup_test.go`. `TestRunRunnerSetup_AgentFlagIsPromptless` stubs the resolver's worst case (no configured provider, two candidates, terminal available) with the picker and the settings writer both failing the test if reached, and asserts the named agent is called once and no local settings are written. `TestRunRunnerSetup_AgentRequiresAProviderMode` pins the rejection for the two provider-free modes.

Nothing edited yet, so here is my read on each point.

**Point 1, `-y` "without asking".** Agree, and this is the line that closes finding 1. The suggested text works. I would trim it a little: "Create the default runners if missing and tailor them to this repo; add --agent to skip the provider choice too". Once that lands I would resolve the finding with a one-line reply pointing at this PR.

**Point 2, `--print-prompt` creating files.** That is finding 2 and it is Soph's line from #2272, not something this PR introduced. Two ways to handle it:

- Fix it here, as the reviewer suggests. Cheapest, and it keeps one PR touching that help block. The cost is that this PR now carries a fix unrelated to `--agent`, and if #2272 edits those lines before merging, this branch conflicts on rebase.
- Leave it to #2272 and rebase after. Cleaner separation, slower.

Since the reviewer asked for it here and it is two lines of text, I lean towards fixing it here and saying so in the PR description. Your call.

**Point 3, the gate versus the messages.** The reviewer is right and it is my defect. `needsProvider` is true for the interactive "tailor" choice too, so `entire runner setup --agent codex` in a terminal works with no `-y`. My flag help and error both say "requires --yes or --dry-run", which is the wrong rule. There is a small design fork hiding here:

- Keep the gate, fix the words. Messages say "only for runs that tailor: --yes, --dry-run, or choosing to tailor at the prompt". One leftover oddity: pass `--agent`, then pick "generic defaults only" at the prompt, and you get the usage error after answering.
- Make `--agent` imply tailoring, so the picker is skipped. Removes the oddity but couples two flags and quietly turns `--agent` into a second `-y`.

I would keep the gate and fix the words. The oddity is a user contradicting themselves and the error names it.

**Non-blocking, the model.** Correct. The override path calls `buildCheckpointSummaryProvider(name, "")`, so the agent's own default model is used and a configured `summary_generation.model` is ignored. It matters only when `--agent` names the same agent that is already configured, in which case `--agent` is redundant anyway. A `--model` flag would fix it properly, but that is scope creep for both this and dispatch, so I would note it in the PR under "not in this PR".

Which of the forks in points 2 and 3 do you want to settle differently? If none, I will apply all three text changes, re-run tests and lint, and push.

content.text:
Here is the deeper look. The help-text gap is the visible symptom, but reading the code path shows a second, worse effect underneath it.

**What `--print-prompt` actually does in a fresh repo**

1. `writesRunnerFiles()` is true for it, so `createDefaultRunners` runs and writes the six default files.
2. That function prints one `created .entire/runners/trail-*.json` line per file to the command's stdout writer.
3. The prompt is then printed to the same stdout writer.
4. The "Created 6 default runner(s)…" summary and the "paste the prompt above" hint go to stderr.

So the disclosure problem is two problems:

- **The help does not say files are written.** Line 117 in the Long text and the flag help at line 145 describe printing only. `-y` says "if missing", `--defaults-only` says "create", `--dry-run` says "write nothing". `--print-prompt` is the one mode whose text is silent about its write, which contradicts the PR's own principle that each mode declares whether it writes.

The check is `opts.agent != "" && !mode.needsProvider()`. `needsProvider` is true for `setupModeAdapt` and `setupModeDryRun`. Adapt is reached three ways: `-y`, the deprecated `--run`, or choosing "tailor" at the interactive prompt. So `--agent` is accepted for `-y`, `--dry-run`, and a terminal run where the user picks tailoring. It is rejected for `--defaults-only`, `--print-prompt`, and a terminal run where the user picks "generic defaults only".

**Where the messages are wrong**

Both the flag help at line 149 and the error at line 186 say `--agent` requires `--yes` or `--dry-run`. Against the cases:

| invocation | what happens | what the message implies |
| --- | --- | --- |

| `setup --agent codex` in a terminal, pick defaults only | error after answering: "pass it with --yes or --dry-run" | the fix offered is a different flag, when the real cause is the answer just given |

content.text:
Both create the six default runner files when the repo has none. The difference is what happens after that.

| | `-y` | `--defaults-only` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| creates the defaults if missing | yes | yes |
| gathers repo signal (docs, PRs, checkpoints, trail findings) | yes | no |
| calls a model | yes, one call through your summary provider or `--agent` | never |
| rewrites `prompt.template` in each runner file | yes, tailored to this repo | no, files stay generic |
| in a repo that already has runners | re-tailors them in place | prints "Nothing to do" |
| needs network or an installed agent | yes | no |

So `--defaults-only` is the offline, deterministic half: you get working generic evaluators and nothing else runs. `-y` is the full action: the same files, then a model rewrites their prompts so the score bands and dimensions reflect this repo. The generic set is committable as is, and `-y` can be run later to tailor it, which is why `--defaults-only` ends with a hint pointing at `-y`.

message.content: what d u really mean by? yes, one call through your summary provider or --agent

content.text:
It means `-y` sends exactly one prompt to one AI agent installed on your machine, and there are two ways the CLI decides which agent that is.

**Your summary provider.** The agent named in `summary_generation.provider` in `.entire/settings.local.json`. If that key is set, `-y` uses it with no question asked. If it is not set, the CLI looks at which agents are installed and behaves as described earlier: one installed means it is used and saved, several installed means the picker in a terminal or the alphabetical first without one.

**`--agent <name>`.** The flag this PR adds. It bypasses that whole lookup, uses the named agent for this run, and saves nothing.

Either way the mechanics are the same. The CLI builds one large prompt containing the six current templates and the gathered repo brief, runs the agent's binary headlessly, for example `claude -p` or `codex exec`, and reads back one JSON object mapping runner ids to rewritten templates. "One call" is literal: a single invocation covers all six runners, not one per runner. `--dry-run` makes the same single call and only differs in printing a diff instead of writing.

What the phrase does not mean: no Entire-hosted model is involved, the CLI holds no API key, and the agent runs with whatever credentials it already has on your machine.

message.content: so -y is sending a prompt to my aagent?

content.text:
Yes. `-y` runs your locally installed coding agent once, in headless mode, with a prompt the CLI assembled. Concretely, on this branch:

1. Creates the six default files if the repo has none.
2. Picks the agent, from `summary_generation.provider`, from `--agent`, or by the lookup described earlier.
3. Gathers a brief about the repo.
4. Builds one prompt containing that brief and the six current templates.
5. Executes the agent's binary with that prompt and waits for its text.
6. Parses the returned JSON and rewrites `prompt.template` in each runner file it changed.

That costs whatever a single call to that agent costs on your account, and it takes as long as the agent takes to answer. If you want to see the exact prompt before it is sent, `--print-prompt` writes it to stdout instead of sending it, and `--debug-dir DIR` saves both the prompt and the raw response for a run that does send it.
